title: A lake with no river
teaches: What an ice sheet leaves behind, how to read it from shaded relief, and how the land rises once the ice is gone

parts.title: The footprint of an ice sheet

blocks.text: At the last glacial maximum, about 21,000 years ago, ice covered almost all of Canada and the northern edge of the United States. The Laurentide ice sheet, centred over Hudson Bay, was up to about 3 kilometres thick and reached south past where New York, Chicago and Cincinnati now stand. To the west, the smaller Cordilleran ice sheet filled the mountains of British Columbia and pushed a tongue of ice, the Puget lobe, south down the Puget Lowland past Seattle, where it was about a kilometre thick.

An ice sheet is a glacier on a continental scale, and it does the same things as the Rhône glacier of lesson 13, only over hundreds of thousands of square kilometres. It scrapes and polishes the ground, carries rock and soil, and drops them. Beneath the ice it smears out a dense layer of unsorted clay, sand and boulders called **till**. In front of it, meltwater streams spread sheets of sorted sand and gravel called **outwash**, sorted by the water just as the river sorted grains in lesson 2. When it melts away it leaves a landscape that can be read, if you know what to look for.

Much of that landscape is hidden by fields, forests and towns. Since the 2000s, though, aircraft carrying **lidar**, a laser rangefinder that sends out hundreds of thousands of pulses a second, have mapped the bare ground of whole states to within a few centimetres, seeing through gaps in the trees. Shaded by a computer from an imaginary sun, the results show landforms that people walking over them never noticed.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: About 21,000 years ago ice sheets up to 3 km thick covered Canada and the northern United States, including the Puget Lowland.
Ice leaves till, a dense, unsorted mix of clay, sand and boulders, beneath it, and meltwater spreads sorted outwash sand and gravel in front of it.
Lidar maps the bare ground from the air, revealing glacial landforms hidden under trees and fields.

blocks.text: Between Rochester and Syracuse in western New York, the farmland is covered by thousands of low, smooth hills, all pointing the same way. They are **drumlins**, from the Irish word for a little ridge: oval hills of till and older sediment, typically a kilometre or two long and a few tens of metres high, shaped like an upturned spoon or the back of a whale. The New York field holds around 10,000 of them, one of the largest in the world. The Puget Lowland has them too, and Seattle's hills, running north to south, owe their shape to the same process.

Drumlins form under moving ice, which moulds the sediment of its bed into streamlined shapes, the way a river shapes sand bars. They line up with the direction the ice moved, and most have a blunter, steeper end facing up-ice and a long tapering tail pointing down-ice. How exactly they form is still argued about, but they are among the most reliable indicators of which way the ice flowed.

blocks.caption: Shaded relief of farmland near Palmyra, New York, from heights measured from the air. Move the sun to light the ground from a different direction.
blocks.task: Light the drumlins so they stand out

blocks.text: The effect of the light is the reason shaded-relief maps are drawn with a choice of sun. A slope facing the light is bright and a slope facing away is dark. Light that runs along a ridge lights both its sides equally and it almost disappears; light from across it makes it stand out sharply. Geologists looking for drumlins, old shorelines or the scarps of faults (lesson 16) shade the same ground from several directions, so that nothing is hidden by an unlucky choice of sun.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Drumlins are streamlined hills of glacial sediment, aligned with the ice flow, usually with a blunt up-ice end.
In shaded relief, landforms show most clearly when lit from across their long axes.

blocks.text: Many glaciated landscapes are dotted with small round lakes and hollows that have no stream flowing in or out. Henry David Thoreau's Walden Pond, in Massachusetts, is one; Seattle's Green Lake is another. They are called **kettles**, and they come from ice that was left behind.

As an ice sheet shrinks, it does not always retreat neatly. Its edge thins and breaks up, and large blocks of stagnant ice are cut off from the main sheet. Meltwater streams flowing off the ice bury these blocks in outwash sand and gravel. Insulated beneath the debris, a buried block can take decades or centuries to melt. When it finally does, the ground above slumps into the space it leaves, forming a steep-sided hollow. If the hollow reaches below the water table, it fills with groundwater and becomes a lake, fed and drained through the gravel rather than by streams.

blocks.caption: How a kettle forms: a stranded block of ice is buried in outwash by meltwater, melts slowly, and leaves a hollow that fills with groundwater.

blocks.text: On central Whidbey Island, outwash plains pitted with kettles form some of the island's best farmland; the Whidbey Island branch of this course explores them. A field of kettles shows where an ice sheet's edge stagnated and broke up, rather than retreating smoothly.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Kettles form where blocks of stagnant ice, buried in outwash, melt and the ground collapses into the space.
Kettle lakes are fed and drained by groundwater, often with no stream in or out.

blocks.text: An ice sheet is heavy enough to bend the Earth. Lesson 5 described continental crust floating on the denser mantle beneath it, like a barge on water. Load the barge and it sits lower. Ice is about 0.3 times as dense as mantle rock, so a sheet 3 kilometres thick pushes the crust down by about 900 metres, as the mantle beneath slowly flows aside. When the ice melts, the crust rises again, but the mantle flows back slowly, over thousands of years.

blocks.caption: Crust floating on the mantle, loaded by an ice sheet and rising after it melts. The rebound in this simplified model slows as it goes, as it does in reality.
blocks.task: Load the crust with at least 1.5 km of ice, melt it, and let at least 8,000 years pass

blocks.text: So the land around Hudson Bay, where the Laurentide ice was thickest, is still rising, by about a centimetre a year, more than 8,000 years after the ice left. Beaches that were at sea level when the ice melted now stand far up the hillsides, in long flights of old shorelines. In Sweden, on the High Coast of the Gulf of Bothnia, the highest such shoreline is nearly 300 metres above today's sea. Around the Puget Sound, marine shells and clays laid down when the ice first left lie well above sea level today, lifted by the same rebound.

The ice ages, in other words, have not quite finished with the land. That is a fitting place for the trunk of the course to turn, from the slow processes of the earlier lessons toward the sudden ones: faults that snap, volcanoes that explode, and coastlines that drop in an afternoon.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: An ice sheet presses the crust down by about 0.3 times its own thickness.
After the ice melts, the crust rises over thousands of years as the mantle flows back; Hudson Bay is still rising about 1 cm a year.
Raised beaches record how far the land has risen since the ice left.

blocks.caption: Five questions on what the ice left
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: A drumlin has a steep, blunt north end and a long tail tapering south. Which way did the ice move?
items.why: Drumlins usually face their blunt end up-ice and their tail down-ice, so the ice came from the north.

items.ask: On a shaded-relief map, a set of ridges running north to south almost disappears. Where is the light probably coming from?
choices: The north or the south, along the ridges
The east or the west, across the ridges
items.why: Light along a ridge lights both its sides equally, so it shows little contrast. Light from across it makes one side bright and the other dark.

items.ask: How does a kettle lake form?
choices: A buried block of glacial ice melts, the ground collapses into the space, and groundwater fills the hollow
A river is dammed by a moraine
A meteorite strikes the outwash plain
items.why: Kettles are collapse hollows left by stranded ice buried in outwash; groundwater fills those that reach below the water table.

items.ask: An ice sheet 2 km thick sits on the crust for thousands of years. Roughly how far does it push the crust down?
items.why: Ice is about 0.3 times as dense as mantle rock, so the crust sinks by about 0.3 times the ice thickness: 0.3 × 2,000 m is 600 m.

items.ask: Why is Hudson Bay still rising, more than 8,000 years after the ice melted?
choices: The mantle flows back beneath it slowly, over thousands of years
New ice is forming beneath it
items.why: The mantle behaves like a very thick fluid on long timescales, so the rebound is slow and is not finished yet.

learned: Ice sheets leave till beneath them and outwash in front of them, and shape their beds into drumlins aligned with the ice flow.
In shaded relief, landforms show most clearly when lit from across their long axes.
Kettle lakes form where buried blocks of stagnant ice melt and the ground collapses.
An ice sheet presses the crust down by about 0.3 times its thickness, and the land rises slowly for thousands of years after it melts.
